cards.explanation: The answer is that he loses courage. When Ish-bosheth heard Abner had died in Hebron, the text says "…he lost courage…" Abner was the army commander who had put him on the throne (2 Samuel 2:8-9), so I think the news hit him hard. Picture the one holding your whole plan together suddenly gone. Nobody's knees stay steady after that.
The answer is False. The text says Ish-bosheth "…lost courage, and all Israel was dismayed." So he had company, friends. The whole nation was dismayed too.

The answer is Benjamin. Baanah and Rechab are "…of the tribe of Benjamin…" The text says Beeroth is considered part of Benjamin, and their father Rimmon is called a Beerothite. A name and a tribe, all packed in one verse.

The answer is that he falls and becomes lame. His nurse picked him up and ran, but "…as she was hurrying to escape, he fell and became lame." He was five years old, and the text says he was lame in his feet. It's a sad little detail to find in the middle of this chapter, friends.
The answer is Mephibosheth. The text introduces him quickly here, just as the boy who fell. Hang on to the name, friends, because David speaks to him later (2 Samuel 9:6).
The answer is nap. The text says Rechab and Baanah came in the heat of the day, "…while the king was taking his midday nap." This is a heavy part of the story, and I think it's a hard one to read.

The answer is to get some wheat. That's the cover story. They entered the interior of the house "…as if to get some wheat…" It's a plain, ordinary errand. The text says that's how it looked, and then they stabbed him in the stomach.

The answer is True. The text says they "…traveled all night by way of the Arabah." Their destination was David at Hebron. They went all night with no stops mentioned, carrying what they had taken from the king.

The answer is Hebron. They brought it "…to David at Hebron…" That's where David was anointed king over Judah (2 Samuel 2:4), and it's where Abner died. A lot of this story keeps coming back to one city, bakers.

The answer is that the LORD granted him vengeance on Saul's family. That's what they claim. They say, "Today the LORD has granted vengeance to my lord the king against Saul and his offspring." They say the LORD did this for David. David's answer, though, shows he doesn't take it that way.

The answer is False. David says someone told him "Look, Saul is dead…" and thought he was bringing good news. David seized him and put him to death at Ziklag. That was his reward, in David's words, not a gift.

The answer is righteous. That's the word David uses. He says wicked men killed "…a righteous man in his own house and on his own bed…" He calls what they did wicked and he calls Ish-bosheth righteous. Those are David's words, and he says them to the two men standing in front of him.

The answer is that they bury it in Abner's tomb in Hebron. David's young men "…took the head of Ish-bosheth and buried it in Abner’s tomb in Hebron." Abner was the commander who made Ish-bosheth king (2 Samuel 2:8-9), so the two ended up together. I think that's a quiet, careful ending to a hard scene. And friends, the story isn't over.
